notes.text: I'm going to begin by pulling up the mission briefing.

I'm planning how to get the wind and drag values: measuring at several altitudes from the aircraft gives the wind speed, shear, direction, and veer directly, with noise. Drag will come from fall time and impact, and the updraft from drops through smoke at the calibration fire.

I'm now setting up the first test drops: three releases away from the smoke, at 100, 150, and 30 meters, so I can isolate drag before going through the plume. Fall time and horizontal travel should give the drag estimate, and the release points are placed so the wind drift still keeps the loads clear of the smoke.

I'm checking the drag estimate: a 100 m drop in 7.2 s with only 18.7 m of northward drift suggests drag is fairly high, so the load is close to terminal velocity. Working from the average speed, I'd put the drag coefficient somewhere around 0.04 to 0.06. I'm also noting the wind readings at 30, 100, and 150 m, which shift in speed and direction as altitude rises.

I'm working out the wind shear from the speeds at 100, 150, and 30 m, which comes to about 0.28. The direction veer works out to roughly 5 degrees, though with around 4 degrees of noise on each reading that's uncertain. I'm setting up a first hypothesis with drag at 0.05, surface wind at 10.7 m/s from 206°, shear 0.28, and veer 5, then comparing it against the data.
The fall times are running too long, which points to drag being set too high. I'll try lowering it to 0.03.

Checking the drag adjustment for test 1 again, I get roughly 0.028 at dt=0.13, and test 2 lands near 0.027 by the same method. Test 3 comes out lower, around 0.022, which makes sense given the 0.05 s noise means it responds less to dt changes.

Working through the y-direction drag fit, test 1 suggests about 0.0265 and test 2 about 0.0274. Test 3 runs the opposite way, heading south, and pulls the estimate down to around 0.0236, though wind could be affecting that too, so I'll try drag at 0.027.

The residuals look close to noise level, though the second test's vertical offset is running a bit high. I'm checking whether wind is what's driving that: with high drag the load should follow the wind fairly closely, and the wind direction works out to roughly 206 degrees, giving x and y components of about -4.7 and -9.6. A predicted vertical offset that's too positive would mean the model is placing the load too far north, which points toward either more southward wind or more drag. The first test sits at 1.6, while the second, higher up with more shear, is at 3.9.

Now I'm planning updraft tests, since that's the main unknown left, and I'll release drops through the smoke column to see how much the updraft slows the load and pushes it off course near the end.

I'm going to run a couple of updraft drops: one from altitude 100 at speed 60 heading 0 aimed at the origin, and one from altitude 50 at speed 50 heading 90. For the second I want a rough sense of how far it travels forward before it reaches the smoke, so I'll simulate that.

I'm checking the drop results: with updraft 5, a release from the origin lands at (54.1, -26.5), and a release at (-54, 26) would land near the origin. Next I'll run two more drops: test 4 at heading 0, altitude 100, speed 60 landing near (24.7, -18.7), and test 5 at heading 90, altitude 50, speed 50 from (-54, 26).

I'm checking the smoke-test fall times against the no-smoke baseline, and the updraft-5 run lands close to the simulator's predicted 4.8 s. Then I'm turning to the wind readings at 50 m and 100 m to compare them.

I'm working out what the 50 m reading implies: with a shear exponent of 0.28, the 10.5 m/s at 100 m would predict about 8.6 m/s at 50 m, but the measured 9.4 suggests a weaker shear closer to 0.16, given roughly 0.5 m/s of noise.
The predicted fall time is too long, which means the updraft is weaker than 5, so I'll try a value of 3 next.

I'm checking the zero-crossing for test 4 and test 5 to estimate the updraft, which comes out near 3.25, and then estimating the vertical position at that point.

All five y-residuals come out positive, averaging about +2.3 m, so the model keeps predicting too far north. That points to wind needing a stronger southward component, so I'm considering raising the wind speed to around 11.0.

I'm weighing a small bump in wind speed, around 0.27 m/s more southward, which over the first seven seconds would shift the drift by roughly 1.5 m. Changing the wind direction toward 200° would push the x-residual well off, so speed is the better lever. I'm comparing the measured wind values near 10.5 against the per-test residuals, which grow with altitude and look strongest at 150 m.

I'm trying wind speed 11.1 together with the updraft at 3.25, and I'll adjust the shear and veer later. The goal is to get the predictions at the hotspots within about 2 m.

I'm checking test 2's dx of -3.5, which predicted too far west. At the 150 altitude, the direction is 206 plus 2.5, giving 208.5, and the measured value there is 208. I'm working through how the x component of the wind depends on direction to see whether lowering veer would reduce the westward drift.

I'm weighing whether reducing the direction at 150 m would ease the westward drift seen in test 2, but a negative veer would push test 5 further west, so that trade-off is a problem. The residuals are now around 1.7 m, close to the expected noise level, so the remaining five test drops should go toward the altitudes and headings that matter most for hotspot updrafts.

I'm planning the remaining test drops to cover high speed at 80, low speed at 45, and both easterly and westerly headings, with some passes through smoke to help pin down the updraft. For test 6 I'm considering altitude 150, speed 80, heading 270, aiming through the smoke, and I'm working out how far the quadratic drag carries it.

I'm estimating where to release a test drop through the smoke at altitude 150, speed 80, heading 270, using rough drag and wind-drift numbers to get an approximate release point. That puts it around (163, 99), but the smoke radius is 50, so I want to run a proper simulation to confirm the aim.

I'm noting that enters_smoke comes out true even when the release starts at the origin, since it's released above the fire. Test 6, released at offset (137.9, 86.7), will land roughly at the origin, so the smoke effect shifts slightly but that's acceptable. Test 7 starts at offset (-31.9, -22.5).

I'm comparing the wind readings: at 150 it's 11.3 at 201 now versus 11.9 at 208 earlier, and at 30 it's 8.6 at 206 against 7.5 at 201. These look like measurement noise, so I'm going to hold off on changing the current hypothesis.

I'm checking test 6 at 150 m, which has a similar offset to test 2: the predicted landing is too far west and north, so the observed point is more east and south. Since both high-altitude tests at 150 m show the same bias, I'm reasoning that the wind aloft should push the drop more east-south, toward the 206 (SSW) direction, and I'm framing the error as observed minus predicted.

I'm working through the wind correction: the error vector points roughly 4.7 m perpendicular to the wind direction, which suggests the upper-altitude wind should be veering in the opposite sense from what the model assumes. I'm considering lowering the veer parameter to see how it shifts the 150 m and 30 m directions, while noting that the short low-altitude drops would respond differently.

I'm checking whether the 150 m drops need the wind veer adjusted. Spread over the fall, the mismatch works out to roughly an 8° rotation in the 100–150 m band, but adjusting veer linearly would also shift the lower-altitude drops in the wrong direction, so I'm looking at whether a wind-direction offset plus veer could fit both.

I'm now checking whether a combined shift in wind direction and veer can fit both the 100 m and 150 m drops, since a linear veer alone would disturb the lower-altitude ones. Working through the time-weighted average, the 150 m drops need roughly a 2.7° rotation while the 100 m drops stay put, which works out to a wind direction near 200.6 and a veer near -5.8.

I'm checking whether a wind direction near 201 with veer at -6 fits the measured drops, since the mean directions at 30 to 50 m sit around 203 and the noise is a few degrees per measurement.

I overshot badly: the test 2 and test 6 shifts came out near 9 and 11 points, far more than I expected. My sensitivity estimate was off. I'll linearize around the current point, treating the two parameter changes as Δa = -5 and Δb = -11, though they're hard to separate this way.

I'm going to perturb one parameter at a time to estimate the Jacobian, starting from the base point (206, 5). The first perturbation sets wind direction to 201 and keeps veer at 5, and then I'll compute the result.

I'm working through the wind_dir -5 effects for each test, where the shifts in dx and dy are mostly positive in x and negative in y. Now I'm moving on to the veer -11 comparison from P1 to P2, starting with test1's small shift.

I'm setting up the normal equations by computing the sum of squares for the wind_dir and veer effects on dx and dy, starting with the A terms.

Still summing the squared values and cross terms for dx and dy to get the combined totals for the normal equations.

Now I'm finishing the dx and dy totals for the V terms, which come to about -13.6 combined. Then I'm setting up the solve for α and β with the two normal equations.

Now I'm plugging the solved values back in: α comes out near 0.37 and β near 0.36, which gives the shifts in wind_dir and veer. Then I'm checking each test's predicted dx residual against its base value.

I'm checking the predicted dx and dy residuals for each test against the fitted shifts, and they look reasonable. Test 5's dy residual of about 2.2 stays high, so I'm noting it as a persistent outlier. The measured average wind direction lands near 203, which fits the fitted value of about 204.

I'm settling on the veer value of about 1 now, so I'll compare the fit at a wind direction of 204.1 with that veer setting.

Noise level looks fine now, so I'm moving on to the other parameters: drag, wind speed, shear, and updraft. That leaves three test drops. Hotspots may need higher intensities up to 1.4 and a larger updraft, and since updraft is set by tests 4 through 7, I'll run a sensitivity check at an updraft of 3.25 to see how the residuals shift.

I'm going to use the last three test drops on extremes: a high-altitude, fast run through the smoke, a low-altitude heading into the wind, and one at an intermediate heading, since the earlier tests mostly covered headings 0, 90, 180 and 270. The aim is more data to tighten the parameter estimates.

I'm comparing the predicted landing times with the observed ones, and test 10 stands out with a roughly 16 m miss on landing position. Tests 8 and 9 came in close to their predictions.

The landing miss on test 10 doesn't fit the updraft pattern from the other tests. Without any updraft, a fall from 140 m should take about 9.3 s, and the observed 9.48 s is barely above that. Meanwhile, the smoke seemed to slow tests 4 and 8 considerably, so the model's updraft profile might be fine and the load could have drifted out of the column quickly.

I'm checking whether test 10's landing miss is just a sim-versus-observed mismatch, so I'll run the comparison with the current updraft hypothesis and look at the residuals for all ten tests before refitting.

Checking the simulated release from the origin against the offset release: the comparison looks fine, with test 10 off by about -4.1 in y and test 9 off by 2.7 in x. Next I'm working out the residual means across the ten tests to refine the fit with all parameters.

I'm reading the residuals as mostly noise, with mean dy around -0.35. I'll test sensitivity next by perturbing updraft, drag, wind speed, and shear, since the outliers at test 10 and test 9 are the main open question.

I'm setting up the Jacobian columns for dx, dy, and dt, one per perturbation step, and I've got the base residuals for the six test points to work from.

Now I'm filling in the U, D, and W perturbation tables row by row, with the last W row cut off.

Now I'm working through the S perturbation table, which is the shear step at +0.1 for all ten test points. I noticed W and S are nearly collinear for some tests but still distinct, and I'm considering how raising wind speed and raising shear might combine across altitudes.

I'm weighting the dt residuals heavily, since their noise is small compared with the position residuals, and I'm noting that drag and updraft each shift dt in a fairly consistent way, so those two parameters should be pinned down well by the timing data.

Checking the drag and updraft numbers against the timing residuals: the three non-smoke tests average out near zero, and the smoke tests come to about -0.004, so drag and updraft look well pinned down. The position misfit is left for wind, shear, direction and veer to explain, with tests 10 and 5 standing out.

I'm weighing the W and S columns against the test 10 and test 5 residuals, since nudging wind down would make test 10's dy less negative but also push test 5 up. I'm setting up a least-squares fit on dx and dy for those two parameters, holding drag fixed because the timing data already pins it down.

Now I'm computing the sums of squares for the W and S columns over the dx entries, since the least-squares normal equations need those terms.

Now I'm summing the squared W and S entries over both dx and dy, and starting the cross-product terms for the normal equations.

Now I'm finishing the cross-product sums for W against the dx and dy residuals, then doing the same for S, so the normal equations have all their terms.

Now I'm solving the two-by-two system for the wind and shear changes, which gives a wind step of about -0.38 and a shear step of about -0.45. Scaled to the actual parameter units, that's roughly -0.19 m/s on wind speed and -0.045 on shear, and I'm starting to check the expected residuals with those values.

Now I'm checking the predicted dx and dy residuals for the first few test points against the updated wind and shear values.

Now I'm checking the predicted residuals against the data, and the total squared error in dx drops from about 16.6 before the update, while dy goes from about 33.1 down only slightly, so the gain is marginal.

Now I'm checking how the residual sums come out after the fit, and they land near the noise level, so the improvement is real but there's nothing more to squeeze from those two parameters.

Now I'm comparing the measured wind speeds at the higher levels against the updated wind and shear, which come out a bit low at 140 and 150 meters but close overall. Next I'm fitting the shear exponent from the logged speeds and heights to see whether the profile matches.

Now I'm computing the mean of the measured wind speeds and the mean of their logged values, then working through the deviations from each mean for the shear fit.

Now I'm comparing the drop-based wind and shear values against the measurement-based fit, which gives a slightly lower wind speed and a shear exponent close to the same range, and I'm wondering whether drag is partly trading off against wind speed here.

Now I'm checking the measured wind directions against the veer fit, which lines up within a degree or two at most heights. With wind speed and shear moved to about 10.9 and 0.235, I want to recheck direction, veer and drag together, starting from the drag value of 0.027.

Now I'm checking the direction, veer and updraft values together, with the shear set to about 0.235.

I'm checking the mean displacement values, which come out to about 0.2 in x and 0.03 in y, and both look consistent with the linear prediction. I'm also noting a working hypothesis with drag at 0.027, ws at 10.9, and direction at 204.1, with shear still to be considered.

I'm settling on a hypothesis with a shear of 0.235, a veer of 1, and an updraft of 3.25, and I'm about to start the operation.

I'm weighing parameter choices, leaning toward mid-range values or settings like the tests. Simulating from the origin looks risky, since the calibration fire there may still be burning and its smoke would skew the result. I'm considering releasing at a guessed point closer to the target instead.

I'm settling on parameter values for each target, mostly at the lower end of the altitude range and a lower speed to cut down on drift and drag sensitivity. I'm also planning to start the release point near each target and correct it iteratively.

I'm working out a first guess for the release point: at altitude around 72 with speed 52, the forward travel comes to roughly 80 m, and wind pushes the drop southwest by a similar margin over the fall time.

I'm working out the forward travel and wind drift for the first target, which puts the release point at about (-957, 532).

I'm correcting the release positions for three targets by applying the measured impact errors, starting with T1 and T2 whose new release coordinates I've already worked out.

I'm working through the remaining targets T4 and T5, applying their offsets to get new release points, and noting that the corrected shots should have less smoke exposure, so these offsets will need another pass.

I'm going through the remaining position corrections one by one: T1 is already right, and the others still show offsets of a few tenths of a meter up to about three meters for T5.

I'm also weighing whether to hedge against parameter uncertainty by averaging predictions across a few plausible hypotheses, but the drop-based fit looks stronger, so I'll apply the corrections directly and double-check T5 and T3.

The temperature at T5 checks out at 0.4 m. Next I want to confirm T1 holds up too, since its intensity of 1.38 sits beyond the measured range and would be an extrapolation from the updraft data. Running a sensitivity case under the alternative hypothesis would show the spread, but it isn't needed, so I'll leave it out.
